title: A good heart (Avot 2:9)
hookLine: Yochanan ben Zakkai asks his students the best path; the answer that wins is a good heart
carry: everything else grows from the heart
tomorrow: repent a day before you die

cards: A teacher gives his five students one assignment. No test, no essay. Just: go out and look at the world, then come back and tell me the one good path a person should hold on to.

Five students, five answers. Then the teacher picks one, and explains why it wins. He's Rabban Yochanan ben Zakkai, the student of Hillel, remembered as the sage who kept Jewish learning alive when Jerusalem fell to Rome.
The winning answer is two Hebrew words: lev tov.

teach.h: GO OUT AND SEE THE GOOD WAY.
teach.b: Go out and see, he says, which is the good way a person should cling to. The five come back. Rabbi Eliezer says: a good eye, meaning a generous way of looking at people.
Rabbi Joshua: a good friend. Rabbi Yose: a good neighbor. Rabbi Shimon: someone who sees what's coming, who thinks about the results of what they do.
And Rabbi Elazar ben Arach: a good heart. Then the teacher speaks. I prefer the words of Elazar ben Arach, because his words include all of yours.
Why? Generous seeing starts in the heart.
A good friend and a good neighbor are what a good heart becomes when it lives near people.

teach.h: HIS WORDS INCLUDE ALL OF YOURS.
teach.b: Even seeing what's coming depends on caring about who gets hurt.
The heart is the root; the others are branches.
In the Bible's Hebrew, the heart isn't just feelings. It's where a person thinks, decides and wants. So lev tov isn't only warmth.
It's a whole inner life pointed toward the good. Then the Mishnah runs the same exercise backward. Which is the bad way a person should stay away from?
A bad eye, a bad friend, a bad neighbor, someone who borrows and doesn't pay back, and, from Elazar ben Arach again, a bad heart. And again the teacher says: his words include all of yours.

how: This mishnah is studied as a portrait of character, and 'lev tov' is still an everyday Hebrew phrase for a kind, good-hearted person.

o: a good heart: an inner life pointed toward good
a healthy heart from a long, calm life
a warm feeling of love for your family

games.q: who said what — tap the pairs.

s: Yochanan ben Zakkai said all five answers were equal
he preferred a good heart, because it includes all the others.
in biblical Hebrew, the heart is also where a person thinks and decides
lev tov is a whole inner life pointed toward the good.
the Mishnah runs the question backward, asking for the bad way
and the answer that wins is again Elazar's: a bad heart.

games.q: you're Yochanan ben Zakkai. five students bring five good answers. which do you choose, and why?
o: a good friend: people need people.
a good heart: it includes all the others.
games.why: he chose Elazar ben Arach's good heart, saying his words include all of yours.

practice: Put a hand on your chest if that feels natural, and notice the heart going on quietly without you asking it to.

Then walk the four branches: someone you could see more generously, a friend you could reach out to, a neighbor who needs something, one choice today whose results you could think through. Let each one come back to the heart.

wordCard.voice: Lev tov. A good heart: the answer Yochanan ben Zakkai chose, because it holds all the others inside it.

orig.note: Hebrew: a good heart, still an everyday phrase in Israel.

carryVoice: Your line: everything else grows from the heart. Five answers, one root. That's two hundred fifty-seven.
